content: The document outlines the contributions of various experts and organizations in the field of maternal and child health, nutrition, and public health. It highlights the roles of professionals from global institutions, universities, and health organizations in developing guidelines for daily iron and folic acid supplementation in pregnant women. These guidelines aim to improve maternal and infant health outcomes, particularly in settings with varying levels of anemia, malaria prevalence, and nutritional deficiencies. The experts involved include medical officers, technical officers, regional advisers, and researchers from institutions such as the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, universities, and non-governmental organizations. Their work focuses on addressing critical health issues such as severe anemia, maternal mortality, iron deficiency, and neural tube defects in newborns. The guidelines also consider the impact of supplementation on birth weight, gestational age, cognitive performance, and the prevention of adverse effects. The recommendations emphasize the importance of tailoring interventions based on specific population characteristics, such as malaria-endemic regions, HIV status, and the prevalence of anemia or iron deficiency. Subgroup analyses are conducted to determine the optimal timing, dosage, and composition of iron and folic acid supplementation, as well as to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of these interventions. The document also explores the potential benefits of daily iron and folic acid supplementation in improving maternal and infant health outcomes. It addresses key questions regarding the appropriate dosage, frequency, and duration of supplementation, as well as the settings in which these interventions are most effective. The guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations to reduce the burden of anemia and related health complications in pregnant women and their infants.
